claim: Flagella are crucial for bacterial motility and pathogenesis.
source: Flagella are crucial for bacterial motility and pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about flagella function.

claim: The flagellar capping protein (FliD) regulates filament assembly by chaperoning and sorting flagellin (FliC) proteins after they traverse the hollow filament and exit the growing flagellum tip.
source: The flagellar capping protein (FliD) regulates filament assembly by chaperoning and sorting flagellin (FliC) proteins after they traverse the hollow filament and exit the growing flagellum tip.
evidence: This statement describes the known function of FliD based on established scientific understanding.

claim: In the absence of FliD, flagella are not formed, resulting in impaired motility and infectivity.
source: In the absence of FliD, flagella are not formed, resulting in impaired motility and infectivity.
evidence: This is a general statement about FliD function based on established knowledge.

claim: The crystal structure of FliD from Pseudomonas aeruginosa was determined at 2.2 Å resolution.
source: Here, we report the 2.2 Å resolution X-ray crystal structure of FliD from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the first high-resolution structure of any FliD protein from any bacterium.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental X-ray crystallography data with specific resolution.

claim: The crystal structure of FliD from Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the first high-resolution structure of any FliD protein from any bacterium.
source: Here, we report the 2.2 Å resolution X-ray crystal structure of FliD from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the first high-resolution structure of any FliD protein from any bacterium.
evidence: This claim is based on the novelty of the experimental structure determination and comparison to existing literature.

claim: Pseudomonas FliD exhibits structural similarity to other flagellar proteins at the domain level.
source: Using this evidence in combination with a multitude of biophysical and functional analyses, we find that Pseudomonas FliD exhibits unexpected structural similarity to other flagellar proteins at the domain level
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pseudomonas FliD adopts a unique hexameric oligomeric state.
source: Using this evidence in combination with a multitude of biophysical and functional analyses, we find that Pseudomonas FliD exhibits unexpected structural similarity to other flagellar proteins at the domain level, adopts a unique hexameric oligomeric state
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic, AUC, SAXS, and EM data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pseudomonas FliD depends on flexible determinants for oligomerization.
source: Using this evidence in combination with a multitude of biophysical and functional analyses, we find that Pseudomonas FliD exhibits unexpected structural similarity to other flagellar proteins at the domain level, adopts a unique hexameric oligomeric state, and depends on flexible determinants for oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by HDX-MS and deletion analysis data showing that regions outside the head domain control oligomerization.

claim: FliD oligomer stoichiometries vary across bacteria to complement their filament assemblies.
source: Considering that the flagellin filaments on which FliD oligomers are affixed vary in protofilament number between bacteria, our results suggest that FliD oligomer stoichiometries vary across bacteria to complement their filament assemblies.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed hexameric state of Pseudomonas FliD versus the pentameric state of Salmonella FliD and known variation in filament protofilament numbers.

claim: Many pathogenic bacteria possess flagella that are responsible for cell motility, adherence to host cells, and pathogenicity.
source: Many of these microbes possess flagella, molecular machines responsible for cell motility, adherence to host cells, and pathogenicity (Duan et al., 2013; Haiko and Westerlund-Wikstrom, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Flagella are helix-shaped hollow attachments formed predominantly by thousands of copies of the protein flagellin (FliC).
source: Flagella are helix-shaped hollow attachments formed predominantly by thousands of copies of the protein flagellin (also called FliC), anchored in the bacterial membrane by a hook (or joint) that is attached to the basal body and that is composed of rotary motor proteins (Arora et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a description of flagellar structure based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: A proton motive force typically drives the propeller motion of flagella.
source: A proton motive force typically drives the propeller motion of flagella (Berg, 2003), resulting in swimming motility.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A FliD oligomer forms the cap protein complex that is located at the tip of the flagellar filament.
source: A FliD (also called HAP2) oligomer forms the cap protein complex that is located at the tip of the flagellar filament (Yonekura et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The FliD cap complex controls the distal growth of the filament by regulating the assembly of FliC molecules.
source: This complex controls the distal growth of the filament by regulating the assembly of FliC molecules, which are transported through the hollow filament from the cytoplasm to the tip of the flagellum.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of FliD function.

claim: The Salmonella serovar Typhimurium flagellum-cap complex adopts the shape of a five-legged stool.
source: The dynamic movement of FliD in this assembly was modeled based on low (~26 Å)-resolution cryo-electron microscopic (EM) structures of the Salmonella serovar Typhimurium flagellum-cap complex (Maki-Yonekura et al., 2003; Yonekura et al., 2000, 2003), which adopts the shape of a five-legged stool with flexible leg domains that regulate the assembly of new FliC molecules onto the tip of the growing flagellum (Maki-Yonekura et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous cryo-EM studies.

claim: The plate of the stool in Salmonella FliD is formed by core regions of the FliD molecule.
source: It has been suggested that the plate of the stool is formed by core regions of the FliD molecule, and that disordered/flexible regions form the five leg structures (Vonderviszt et al., 1998) that are known to interact with the FliC filament.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: FliD exhibits low sequence similarity to the flagellar hook proteins and to FliC.
source: FliD exhibits low sequence similarity to the flagellar hook proteins and to FliC.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis, which is standard knowledge in the field.

claim: FliD shares the disordered terminal regions of flagellar hook proteins and FliC.
source: Nevertheless, it shares the disordered terminal regions of these flagellar proteins, a common structural characteristic that is thought to control the polymerization of flagellar proteins and to play an important role in interaction with the FliC filament (Vonderviszt et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The disordered terminal regions of FliD are the most conserved in FliD sequences across bacteria.
source: These regions are the most conserved in FliD sequences across bacteria.
evidence: This is based on sequence conservation analysis.

claim: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of Campylobacter jejuni.
source: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of numerous bacteria, including Campylobacter jejuni (Black et al., 1988)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of Salmonella.
source: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of numerous bacteria, including Campylobacter jejuni (Black et al., 1988), Salmonella (Allen-Vercoe and Woodward, 1999; Marchetti et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of Escherichia coli.
source: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of numerous bacteria, including Campylobacter jejuni (Black et al., 1988), Salmonella (Allen-Vercoe and Woodward, 1999; Marchetti et al., 2004), Escherichia coli (La Ragione et al., 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of Vibrio cholera.
source: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of numerous bacteria, including Campylobacter jejuni (Black et al., 1988), Salmonella (Allen-Vercoe and Woodward, 1999; Marchetti et al., 2004), Escherichia coli (La Ragione et al., 2000), Vibrio cholera (Krukonis and DiRita, 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: Flagellum-mediated motility is crucial for the virulence and pathogenicity of numerous bacteria, including Campylobacter jejuni (Black et al., 1988), Salmonella (Allen-Vercoe and Woodward, 1999; Marchetti et al., 2004), Escherichia coli (La Ragione et al., 2000), Vibrio cholera (Krukonis and DiRita, 2003), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Arora et al., 2005)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Helicobacter pylori is the major causative agent of gastric cancer.
source: as well as the major causative agent of gastric cancer Helicobacter pylori (Kim et al., 1999)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No high-resolution structure of any FliD protein existed prior to this study.
source: To date, however, no high-resolution structure of any FliD protein exists.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the existing literature at the time of publication.

claim: FliD78-405 was generated by deleting the predicted coiled-coil domains on both the N- and C-termini of full length FliD1–474.
source: To facilitate crystallization of FliD from the P. aeruginosa PAO1 strain, we deleted the predicted coiled-coil domains on both the N- and C-termini of full length FliD, which has 474 residues (FliD1–474), to generate the truncated FliD78-405 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for protein construct generation.

claim: FliD78–405 was expressed in E. coli with an N-terminal His6-tag.
source: We expressed FliD78–405 in E. coli with an N-terminal His6-tag and purified it to homogeneity by Ni2+-NTA, size exclusion and anion exchange chromatography.
evidence: This describes the experimental protein expression and purification methods.

claim: Crystals of FliD78–405 were improved by random matrix microseed screening.
source: We improved initially weakly diffracting crystals of FliD78–405 by random matrix microseed screening (Bergfors, 2003), yielding crystals that diffracted to 2.2 Å resolution.
evidence: This describes the experimental crystallization method used.

claim: A seleno-methionine derivative of FliD78–405 with four leucine-to-methionine mutations (FliD78–405/L4–M4) was crystallized for phasing.
source: In the absence of any homologous protein that could be used as a model for molecular replacement, we crystallized a seleno-methionine derivative of FliD78–405 that included four leucine-to-methionine mutations (FliD78–405/L4–M4).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for obtaining phase information.

claim: Residues 80–273 of FliD78–405 were modeled into clear electron density, including all side chains.
source: We modeled residues 80–273 into clear electron density, including all side chains, but observed density of increasingly poor quality in the C-terminus beyond residue 273 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This describes the quality of the crystallographic data and model building.

claim: A single α helix corresponding to residues 274–308 was modeled with incomplete side chain structures.
source: Thus, we were able to model with confidence only a single α helix in this region, corresponding to residues 274–308, with incomplete side chain structures.
evidence: This describes the quality of the crystallographic data and model building.

claim: Crystals of FliD78–405 consisted of an approximate 50:50 mixture of the FliD78–405 protein and a further proteolyzed version with a molecular weight of about 27 kDa.
source: To determine whether the remaining region of the protein actually existed in the crystals and not just in the protein preparation used for crystallization, we analyzed crystals using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) and SDS-PAGE. Both analyses indicated that the crystals consisted of an approximate 50:50 mixture of the FliD78–405 protein used for crystallization and a further proteolyzed version with a molecular weight of about 27 kDa.
evidence: This is based on LC-MS and SDS-PAGE experimental data.

claim: The proteolyzed form of FliD78–405 in crystals corresponds approximately to residues 78–319 of FliD.
source: The N-terminal His6-tag is still detectable by Western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b). Thus, the proteolyzed form corresponds approximately to residues 78–319 of FliD.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular weight and Western blot data.

claim: The 86 residues absent from the C-terminus in a population of FliD proteins are not required for crystal packing.
source: The 86 residues absent from the C-terminus in a population of FliD proteins are clearly not required for crystal packing, suggesting that they are highly flexible even in a crystalline environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystallographic data showing partial proteolysis.

claim: The crystal structure of FliD78–405 consists of two discrete regions: a stable head region and a flexible leg region.
source: Our crystal structure of FliD78–405 reveals that it consists of two discreet regions with distinct conformational properties, corresponding to a stable head region and a flexible and/or disordered leg region (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: The head region of FliD78–405 is comprised of two separate, but entwined, protein domains.
source: The head region is itself comprised of two separate, but entwined, protein domains.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Residues 80–101 of FliD78–405 form two β strands that belong to the first domain (Head 1).
source: Residues 80–101 form two β strands that belong to the first domain (Head 1), the second domain (Head 2) is formed in its entirety by the contiguous residues 104–230, and residues 231–273 then complete the first domain.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: The second domain (Head 2) of FliD78–405 is formed in its entirety by the contiguous residues 104–230.
source: Residues 80–101 form two β strands that belong to the first domain (Head 1), the second domain (Head 2) is formed in its entirety by the contiguous residues 104–230, and residues 231–273 then complete the first domain.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Residues 231–273 of FliD78–405 complete the first domain (Head 1).
source: Residues 80–101 form two β strands that belong to the first domain (Head 1), the second domain (Head 2) is formed in its entirety by the contiguous residues 104–230, and residues 231–273 then complete the first domain.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: The second domain (Head 2) is a loop insertion of the first domain (Head 1).
source: The second domain is, thus, a loop insertion of the first domain.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: The first domain of the head region (Head 1) exhibits high structural similarity (RMSD=2.5 Å) to the FlgK/HAP1/hook filament capping protein of Burkholderia pseudomallei.
source: We searched for structural homologs of these domains in the Protein Data Bank and found that the first domain of the head region (Head 1) exhibits high structural similarity (RMSD=2.5 Å), despite low sequence identity (14%), to the FlgK/HAP1/hook filament capping protein of Burkholderia pseudomallei (PDB code 4UT1; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis using the Protein Data Bank.

claim: The first domain of the head region (Head 1) has low sequence identity (14%) to the FlgK/HAP1/hook filament capping protein of Burkholderia pseudomallei.
source: We searched for structural homologs of these domains in the Protein Data Bank and found that the first domain of the head region (Head 1) exhibits high structural similarity (RMSD=2.5 Å), despite low sequence identity (14%), to the FlgK/HAP1/hook filament capping protein of Burkholderia pseudomallei (PDB code 4UT1; Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The second head region domain (Head 2) exhibits high structural similarity (RMSD=2.7 Å) to the FliC/flagellin protein of P. aeruginosa.
source: Likewise, the second head region domain (Head 2) exhibits high structural similarity (RMSD=2.7 Å), despite low sequence identity (17%), to the FliC/flagellin protein of P. aeruginosa (PDB code 4NX9; Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis using the Protein Data Bank.

claim: The second head region domain (Head 2) has low sequence identity (17%) to the FliC/flagellin protein of P. aeruginosa.
source: Likewise, the second head region domain (Head 2) exhibits high structural similarity (RMSD=2.7 Å), despite low sequence identity (17%), to the FliC/flagellin protein of P. aeruginosa (PDB code 4NX9; Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The leg region of FliD is highly flexible, as indicated by the paucity of electron density corresponding to residues 274–405.
source: In contrast to the head region, the leg region of FliD is highly flexible, as indicated by the paucity of electron density corresponding to residues 274–405 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is based on the quality of electron density in the crystal structure.

claim: The initial α helical structural element of the leg region, corresponding to residues 274–308, extends from the axis of the head region at a nearly perpendicular angle.
source: Despite this, we were able to model the initial α helical structural element, corresponding to residues 274–308, of this region. This helix extends from the axis of the head region at a nearly perpendicular angle, resulting in an L-shaped monomer subunit structure (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: FliD78–405 monomer subunits are arranged in hexamers in the crystal.
source: In the crystal, FliD78–405 monomer subunits are arranged in hexamers, resulting in a shape akin to a six-pointed star when viewed from the top of the FliD oligomer (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: The FliD78–405 hexamer has a minimum inner diameter of 48 Å and a maximal outer diameter of 136 Å.
source: This star shape has a minimum inner diameter of 48 Å and a maximal outer diameter of 136 Å.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the crystal structure.

claim: When viewed from the side, the FliD hexamer appears as a six-legged stool, the legs of which extend 55 Å below the bottom of the head region.
source: When viewed from the side (Figure 2b), the FliD hexamer appears as a six-legged stool, the legs of which extend 55 Å below the bottom of the head region.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Additional crystallographic symmetry results in the stacking of hexamers in alternating head-to-head and leg-to-leg orientations.
source: Additional crystallographic symmetry results in the stacking of hexamers in alternating head-to-head and leg-to-leg orientations (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: The leg-to-leg stacking forms dodecamers, resulting from the helix–helix interaction of the residues 274–302 of stacked molecules and the interaction of residues 303–308 of one FliD78–405 molecule with Head 1 domain of a stacked molecule, burying a surface area of 1362 Å2.
source: The leg-to-leg stacking forms dodecamers, resulting from the helix–helix interaction of the residues 274–302 of stacked molecules and the interaction of residues 303–308 of one FliD78–405 molecule with Head 1 domain of a stacked molecule, burying a surface area of 1362 Å2.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data and surface area calculations.

claim: The formation of dodecamers may be unique to the FliD78–405 fragment.
source: The formation of dodecamers may be unique to the FliD78–405 fragment, as this strand could potentially be replaced by additional N-terminal residues in the full-length FliD1–474 protein.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the crystal structure.

claim: The morphologies observed for Pseudomonas FliD are highly reminiscent of the pentamer/decamer oligomeric organization of Salmonella FliD as determined by low-resolution cryo-EM analysis.
source: All of the morphologies observed for Pseudomonas FliD are highly reminiscent of the pentamer/decamer oligomeric organization of Salmonella FliD as determined by low-resolution cryo-EM analysis (Maki-Yonekura et al., 2003) (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current structure with previously published cryo-EM data.

claim: Pseudomonas FliD measures 136 Å in diameter with a head region that is 30 Å deep and a leg region that is 55 Å long.
source: In our crystal structure, Pseudomonas FliD measures 136 Å in diameter with a head region that is 30 Å deep and a leg region that is 55 Å long
evidence: This is based on measurements from the crystal structure.

claim: Salmonella FliD measures 145 Å in diameter with a head region that is 30 Å deep and a leg region that is 55 Å long.
source: whereas, in the cryo-EM structure, Salmonella FliD measures 145 Å in diameter with a head region that is 30 Å deep and a leg region that is 55 Å long (Maki-Yonekura et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on previously published cryo-EM data.

claim: The hexameric assembly of FliD78–405 occurs in solution as confirmed by negative stain EM class averaging.
source: Thus, we confirmed that the hexameric assembly of FliD78–405 occurs not only in the crystalline environment but also in solution using negative stain EM class averaging (Tang et al., 2007), resulting in an image that clearly exhibits a hexameric assembly (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is based on negative stain EM experimental data.

claim: FliD78–405 oligomerizes up to a dodecameric state as shown by analytical ultracentrifugation.
source: We found that the FliD78–405 fragment that we crystallized oligomerizes up to a dodecameric state (Figure 3b,c), similar to the crystallographic assembly (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on AUC experimental data.

claim: FliD78–405 oligomerizes up to a dodecameric state as shown by crosslinking analyses.
source: We found that the FliD78–405 fragment that we crystallized oligomerizes up to a dodecameric state (Figure 3b,c), similar to the crystallographic assembly (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on chemical crosslinking experimental data.

claim: The radial distribution function calculated from SAXS data of FliD78–405 is characteristic of an oligomeric assembly forming a hollow sphere.
source: Additionally, we collected small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data of FliD78–405, for which the calculated radial distribution function (Figure 3d) is characteristic of an oligomeric assembly forming a hollow sphere (Svergun and Koch, 2003).
evidence: This is based on SAXS experimental data and cited literature on SAXS interpretation.

claim: The SAXS molecular envelope of FliD78–405 superimposes well with the dodecameric FliD78–405 X-ray crystal structure.
source: These data produce a molecular envelope that superimposes well with our dodecameric FliD78–405 X-ray crystal structure (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on SAXS experimental data and comparison with the crystal structure.

claim: Full-length FliD1–474 forms up to hexamers in solution.
source: Full-length FliD1–474, by contrast, forms up to hexamers in solution (Figure 3e,f), which are likely to represent the physiologically relevant oligomerization state of this protein on the tip of the flagellum.
evidence: This is based on AUC and crosslinking experimental data.

claim: The predominant tetrameric species of FliD1–474 in solution may be a stable intermediate on the path to hexamer formation.
source: The predominant tetrameric species in solution identified by AUC may be a stable intermediate on the path to hexamer formation (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the AUC data.

claim: FliD1–474(I167C/D253C) forms a stable, disulfide-bridged hexamer under non-reducing conditions.
source: We found that when two residues within neighboring head domain subunits, I167 and D253, were each mutated to a cysteine residue (Figure 4a) a stable, hexameric full-length FliD1–474(I167C/D253C) resulted under non-reducing conditions, as shown by SDS-PAGE (Figure 4b) and SAXS (Figure 4c) analyses.
evidence: This is based on SDS-PAGE and SAXS experimental data.

claim: The cysteine bridges in FliD1–474(I167C/D253C) result in the expected interfaces between head domains.
source: We also confirmed that the cysteine bridges resulted in the expected interfaces between head domains by employing mass spectrometry to compare the peptide coverage under reducing and non-reducing conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a) and by successfully detecting the correct cysteine bridges (C167–C253) while ruling out non-specific cysteine bridging (C167–C167 and C253–C253) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b–e).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry experimental data.

claim: Swimming motility lost in the ΔfliD strain was restored in both ΔfliD/fliD1–474 and ΔfliD/fliD1–474(I167C/D253C) complementation strains.
source: We found that swimming motility that was lost in the ΔfliD strain was restored in both ΔfliD/fliD1–474 and ΔfliD/fliD1–474(I167C/D253C) complementation strains, similar to our observations in the wildtype Pseudomonas PAO1 strain (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is based on swimming motility assay experimental data.

claim: FliD1–474(I167C/D253C) protein produced by Pseudomonas maintains its hexameric oligomeric state in flagella preparations.
source: In flagella preparations from the ΔfliD/fliD1–474(I167C/D253C) complementation strain, the FliD1–474(I167C/D253C) protein produced by Pseudomonas maintains its hexameric oligomeric state (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on Western blot experimental data.

claim: FliD1–474 does not maintain a stable hexameric complex in flagella preparations from either the wildtype Pseudomonas PAO1 strain or the ΔfliD/fliD1–474 complementation strain.
source: In contrast, subsequent to flagella isolation from live bacteria, FliD1–474 does not maintain a stable hexameric complex in either the wildtype Pseudomonas PAO1 strain or in the ΔfliD/fliD1–474 complementation strain (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on Western blot experimental data.

claim: The ΔfliD transposon strain does not form flagella.
source: The ΔfliD transposon strain does not form flagella, as indicated by the lack of FliC in the analyzed flagella preparations (lane 5 on the stained Western blot membrane, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on Western blot experimental data.

claim: The wildtype and all complementation strains form flagella as indicated by the presence of flagellin/FliC in the purified flagella samples.
source: In comparison, the wildtype and all complementation strains form flagella as indicated by the presence of flagellin/FliC in the purified flagella samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on Western blot experimental data.

claim: FliD that is covalently locked in its hexameric assembly can form functional flagella that allow Pseudomonas bacteria to swim like Pseudomonas with wildtype FliD.
source: Together, these data indicate that FliD that is covalently locked in its hexameric assembly can form functional flagella that allow Pseudomonas bacteria to swim like Pseudomonas with wildtype FliD.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the swimming motility and Western blot data.

claim: The hexamer oligomeric state of Pseudomonas FliD is functional in vivo.
source: Thus, the hexamer oligomeric state of Pseudomonas FliD is functional in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the complementation and swimming motility data.

claim: Salmonella FliD is known to form pentamers when capping the flagellar filament.
source: We also tested whether Salmonella FliD, which is known to form pentamers when capping the flagellar filament, could function as a capping protein for Pseudomonas flagella.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous literature.

claim: Complementation of the PAO1 PW2975 transposon strain with fliD from Salmonella typhimurium did not restore swimming motility.
source: In contrast to the in vivo functional hexameric forms of P. aeruginosa FliD–474, complementation of the PAO1 PW2975 transposon strain with fliD from Salmonella typhimurium (ΔfliD/fliDStyFliDe) did not restore swimming motility (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on swimming motility assay experimental data.

claim: A wildtype PAO1 full-length FliD1–474 encoded by a codon-optimized gene restored swimming motility in the ΔfliD strain.
source: As this clone was codon-optimized for expression in Escherichia coli, we also confirmed that a wildtype PAO1 full-length FliD1–474 encoded by a similarly codon-optimized gene did restore swimming motility in the ΔfliD strain (ΔfliD/fliDPAOfliDe; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on swimming motility assay experimental data.

claim: Pseudomonas flagella may prefer FliD proteins that adopt hexameric rather than pentameric states.
source: Although there exist many possible reasons other than oligomeric state that could explain the inability of Salmonella FliD to functionally complement Pseudomonas, these data suggest that Pseudomonas flagella may prefer FliD proteins that adopt hexameric rather than pentameric states.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the complementation data.

claim: Each interface between head regions of FliD78–405 subunits in the hexamer has a buried surface area of only 665 Å2.
source: Although the FliD78–405 crystal structure exhibits intermolecular contacts between the head regions of FliD78–405 subunits comprising the hexamer, each of these interfaces is small, with a buried surface area of only 665 Å2, and contains few intermolecular contacts (Figure 5a) relative to typical protein–protein interactions (Jones and Thornton, 1996).
evidence: This is based on surface area calculations from the crystal structure.

claim: FliD78–273 (head region only) is present predominantly in the form of monomers (and dimers to a lesser extent) in solution.
source: By AUC (Figure 5b), chemical crosslinking (Figure 5c) and SAXS analysis (Figure 5d), we observed that when FliD lacks the leg region and the N- and C-terminal coiled-coil domains, it is present predominantly in the form of monomers (and dimers to a lesser extent) in solution, but fails to form higher-order oligomers as do the longer versions of FliD that we analyzed.
evidence: This is based on AUC, crosslinking, and SAXS experimental data.

claim: FliD78–273 is entirely monomeric at pH 8.0 and becomes approximately one-third dimeric at pH 5.0.
source: Because different buffer conditions, including changes in pH, have been shown to affect the polymerization states of flagellar filaments (Shibata et al., 2005) and capping proteins (Imada et al., 1998), we performed additional AUC experiments and found that FliD78–273 is entirely monomeric at pH 8.0 and becomes approximately one-third dimeric at pH 5.0; we observed no higher-order oligomers of FliD78–273 regardless of buffer conditions (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on AUC experimental data at different pH values.

claim: FliD78–474 (lacking only the N-terminal coiled-coil domain) is mainly monomeric with a minority of species appearing to dimerize.
source: We also assessed, by chemical cross-linking, the oligomerization states of FliD variants lacking only the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (FliD78–474; Figure 5e) or the C-terminal coiled-coil domain (FliD1–405; Figure 5f). We found them to be mainly monomeric with a minority of species appearing to dimerize, although the latter exhibit weak higher-order oligomerization potential.
evidence: This is based on chemical crosslinking experimental data.

claim: FliD1–405 (lacking only the C-terminal coiled-coil domain) is mainly monomeric with a minority of species appearing to dimerize.
source: We also assessed, by chemical cross-linking, the oligomerization states of FliD variants lacking only the N-terminal coiled-coil domain (FliD78–474; Figure 5e) or the C-terminal coiled-coil domain (FliD1–405; Figure 5f). We found them to be mainly monomeric with a minority of species appearing to dimerize, although the latter exhibit weak higher-order oligomerization potential.
evidence: This is based on chemical crosslinking experimental data.

claim: FliD78–474 and FliD1–405 adopt extended shapes with flexible regions as shown by SAXS analysis.
source: Kratky plots and radial distribution functions calculated from SAXS data of the variants lacking either the N- or C-terminal coiled-coil domain, FliD78–474 or FliD1–405 respectively, reveal that these proteins adopt extended shapes with flexible regions that are clearly represented in the resulting molecular envelopes (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: This is based on SAXS experimental data.

claim: The driving force for hexamerization of Pseudomonas FliD resides in molecular determinants outside of the head region.
source: These data indicate that the driving force for hexamerization of Pseudomonas FliD resides in molecular determinants outside of the head region and, at a minimum, involves residues in the N-terminal and C-terminal coiled-coil domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the oligomerization data of various FliD truncations.

claim: FliD78–405 assembles into dodecamers as shown in the crystal structure, cross-linking experiments and AUC.
source: FliD78–405 is lacking the C-terminal and N-terminal coiled-coil domain but still assembles into dodecamers, as shown in the crystal structure, cross-linking experiments and AUC, which is likely caused by strand replacement in the head region domain 1 and helix–helix (residues 274–308) interaction of stacked molecules (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure, crosslinking, and AUC experimental data.

claim: The head region (residues 80–273) of FliD78–405 adopts a largely stable exchange-protected fold as shown by HDX-MS.
source: We subjected FliD78–405 to H/D exchange for 10 s to 2 hr and observed that the head region (residues 80–273) of FliD78–405 adopts a largely stable exchange-protected fold with greater stability observed for domain 2 relative to that of domain 1.
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: Head domain 2 of FliD78–405 exhibits greater stability relative to head domain 1 as shown by HDX-MS.
source: We subjected FliD78–405 to H/D exchange for 10 s to 2 hr and observed that the head region (residues 80–273) of FliD78–405 adopts a largely stable exchange-protected fold with greater stability observed for domain 2 relative to that of domain 1.
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: The leg region of FliD78–405, particularly residues C-terminal to the α helix observed in the crystal structure, is more disordered or less stable as shown by HDX-MS.
source: The leg region, particularly residues C-terminal to the α helix observed in the crystal structure, is more disordered or less stable (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: Residues linking head domain 1 to the leg helix display cooperative unfolding behavior as indicated by EX1 kinetics.
source: Residues linking head domain 1 to the leg helix display cooperative unfolding behavior as indicated by EX1 kinetics (Weis et al., 2006) that result in double isotopic envelopes (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data showing EX1 kinetics.

claim: All FliD protein fragments produced were folded properly as shown by circular dichroism.
source: The FliD78–405 protein used in these experiments was folded properly as shown by circular dichroism, as were all other FliD protein fragments that we produced (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on circular dichroism experimental data.

claim: Residues 165–225 of FliD exhibit relatively greater stability in FliD78–405 compared to full length FliD1–474.
source: When we used a difference plot to compare the extent of H/D exchange of full length FliD1–474 with that of FliD78–405, we observed that residues 165–225 exhibit relatively greater stability in FliD78–405 (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data comparison.

claim: Residues 165–171 form the interface between the two head region domains in the hexameric complex.
source: Within this stretch of residues in head domain 2 are those residues, 165–171, which form the interface between the two head region domains in the hexameric complex (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Residues 298–324 of FliD exhibit relative stabilization, part of which (residues 300–308) correspond to the β strand replacement in the opposing head region domain 1 that drives dodecamer formation of FliD78–405.
source: We observed an additional region of relative stabilization for residues 298–324, part of which, residues 300–308, correspond to the β strand replacement in the opposing head region domain 1 that drives dodecamer formation of FliD78–405 (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data and crystal structure analysis.

claim: Full-length FliD1–474 at pH 11 is monomeric.
source: Kratky plots calculated from SAXS data of full-length FliD1–474 at pH 11, which is monomeric under these conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), confirms the overall flexible nature of this protein.
evidence: This is based on AUC experimental data at pH 11.

claim: Full-length FliD1–474 exhibits significant conformational flexibility as shown by heterogeneous molecular envelopes calculated from SAXS data.
source: Accordingly, heterogeneous molecular envelopes calculated from SAXS data collected at different concentrations of FliD1–474 also exhibit significant conformational flexibility (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on SAXS experimental data.

claim: The head region, and more specifically head region domain 1, is stabilized by FliD regions outside of the head region.
source: To gain further insight to the dynamics and interactions of the different regions of FliD, we performed HDX-MS experiments with the remaining Pseudomonas FliD fragments that we had generated (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). HDX-MS heat maps show the overall high degree of flexibility of FliD regions outside the head domain (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and difference plots of FliD truncations in comparison to the full length FliD1–474 indicate that the head region, and more specifically head region domain 1, is stabilized by FliD regions outside of the head region (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data comparison.

claim: The N-terminal coiled coil is responsible for stabilization of head region domain 1 and residues between the leg region α helix and the C-terminal coiled coil.
source: Indeed, the N-terminal coiled coil is responsible for this stabilization of head region domain 1, in addition to stabilization of residues between the leg region α helix and the C-terminal coiled coil (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data comparison.

claim: The C-terminal coiled coil predominantly stabilizes residues in the N-terminal coiled coil.
source: Finally, the C-terminal coiled coil predominantly stabilizes residues in the N-terminal coiled coil (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is based on HDX-MS experimental data comparison.

claim: The stabilization of one FliD region by another is most likely to be direct and intramolecular, rather than allosteric and intermolecular.
source: The stabilization of one FliD region by another is most likely to be direct and intramolecular, rather than allosteric and intermolecular, as the full-length protein FliD1–474 adopts predominantly monomeric species under the conditions that we used for HDX-MS analysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on HDX-MS data and AUC data showing monomeric species.

claim: None of the flexible regions of FliD, save the C-terminal 20 residues, are consistently predicted by sequence analysis to be intrinsically disordered.
source: Notably, none of the flexible regions of FliD, save the C-terminal 20 residues, are consistently predicted by sequence analysis to be intrinsically disordered (Figure 8—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is based on computational disorder prediction analysis.

claim: The flexible regions of FliD are inherently capable of adopting a limited number of conformations required to be in an 'on-state' or an 'off-state'.
source: rather, they are inherently capable of adopting a limited number of conformations required to be in an 'on-state' (actively chaperoning and sorting a FliC protein) or an 'off-state' (engaging only structured and previously positioned FliC proteins).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the disorder prediction and HDX-MS data.

claim: The oligomeric states differ between FliD protein assemblies in diverse bacteria.
source: At the gross structural level, our studies show that the oligomeric states differ between FliD protein assemblies in diverse bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Pseudomonas and Salmonella FliD oligomeric states.

claim: Salmonella FliD performs its native flagellar capping function as a pentamer.
source: Since Salmonella FliD performs its native flagellar capping function as a pentamer (Imada et al., 1998; Maki et al., 1998; Vonderviszt et al., 1998; Yonekura et al., 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pseudomonas FliD forms hexamers both in crystals and in solution.
source: We found that Pseudomonas FliD instead forms hexamers both in crystals and in solution.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure, EM, AUC, and SAXS experimental data.

claim: Pseudomonas FliD constrained to its hexameric state by inter-subunit disulfide bonds is functional in vivo, resulting in the formation of flagella and swimming motility.
source: Additionally, we showed that Pseudomonas FliD constrained to its hexameric state by inter-subunit disulfide bonds is functional in vivo, resulting in the formation of flagella and swimming motility.
evidence: This is based on complementation and swimming motility assay experimental data.

claim: Salmonella FliD that assembles as pentamers does not allow flagellar formation and swimming motility in Pseudomonas bacteria.
source: Conversely, Salmonella FliD that assembles as pentamers does not allow flagellar formation and swimming motility in Pseudomonas bacteria.
evidence: This is based on complementation and swimming motility assay experimental data.

claim: The number of protofilaments in flagellar filaments from diverse bacteria ranges, at least, from 11 in Salmonella to seven in Campylobacter.
source: Much like cryo-EM studies of flagellar filaments from diverse bacteria unequivocally showed that the number of protofilaments ranges, at least, from 11 in Salmonella (Yonekura et al., 2003) to seven in Campylobacter (Galkin et al., 2008)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous cryo-EM studies.

claim: The proteins that cap flagellar filaments vary in their oligomeric states.
source: our structural analyses show that the proteins that cap these filaments also vary in their oligomeric states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of Pseudomonas and Salmonella FliD oligomeric states.

claim: The end of the Salmonella filament exhibits a non-planar surface with five indentations.
source: The end of the Salmonella filament exhibits a non-planar surface with five indentations (Yonekura et al., 2000) into which the five legs of the corresponding FliD pentamer have been modeled (Maki-Yonekura et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous cryo-EM studies.

claim: The hexameric FliD structure suggests that the Pseudomonas filament may incorporate an even greater number of protofilaments than does the Salmonella filament.
source: Although no structure of the Pseudomonas filament has been determined even at low resolution, our hexameric FliD structure suggests that it may incorporate an even greater number of protofilaments than does the Salmonella filament.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the hexameric structure of Pseudomonas FliD.

claim: Pseudomonas flagellar filaments have been found to be macroscopically different from those of Salmonella.
source: Indeed, Pseudomonas flagellar filaments have been found to be macroscopically different from those of Salmonella (Shibata et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Each one of the six FliD head regions that appear as discrete lobes when visualized by EM analysis is actually composed of the first and second domains of neighboring monomer subunits.
source: At 2.2 Å resolution, our crystal structure reveals several previously unknown structural features of FliD that are likely to be critical to its function. First, each one of the six FliD head regions that appear as discreet lobes when visualized by EM analysis is actually composed of the first and second domains of neighboring monomer subunits, as opposed to both domains belonging to the same subunit.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure data.

claim: Each domain within the head region exhibits high structural similarity to the corresponding domains of other flagellar proteins, including the hook-filament junction protein/FlgK and flagellin/FliC.
source: Second, despite vanishingly low sequence similarity, each domain within the head region exhibits high structural similarity to the corresponding domains of other flagellar proteins, including the hook-filament junction protein/FlgK and flagellin/FliC.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claim: At least one protein domain from the proteins that occupy the distal ends of the hook (FlgK) and the cap (FliD) adopts a common structural fold.
source: Thus, at least one protein domain from the proteins that occupy the distal ends of the hook (FlgK) and the cap (FliD) adopts a common structural fold, which may be required for and unique to their function at these related positions within the flagellum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity data.

claim: The domain conservation among flagellar proteins confirms a previous study proposing a structural relationship of FliD to other flagellar proteins despite their low sequence similarities.
source: This domain conservation among flagellar proteins confirms a previous study proposing a structural relationship of FliD to other flagellar proteins despite their low sequence similarities (Vonderviszt et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and the current structural data.

claim: The structural conservation suggests that a structurally similar cap complex may form at both hook and on the distal end.
source: This structural conservation suggests that a structurally similar cap complex may form at both hook and on the distal end.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural similarity data.

claim: FliD may play a functional role earlier in the flagellar assembly process, prior to its known FliC sorting function.
source: It also suggests that FliD may play a functional role earlier in the flagellar assembly process, prior to its known FliC sorting function.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural similarity to FlgK.

claim: In mutants of Salmonella that lack filaments, FlgK (HAP1), FliD (HAP2) and FlgL (HAP3) form a layered structure at the distal end of the hook-basal body.
source: Notably, in mutants of Salmonella that lack filaments, FlgK (HAP1), FliD (HAP2) and FlgL (HAP3) form a layered structure at the distal end of the hook-basal body (Homma and Iino, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The shared domain structure of portions of FliC and FliD suggests that the chaperoning activity of FliD could derive from its presentation of a like-structured template against which FliC subunits may fold prior to being positioned into the growing filament.
source: In addition, the shared domain structure of portions of FliC and FliD suggests that the chaperoning activity of FliD could derive, at least in part, from its presentation of a like-structured template against which FliC subunits may fold prior to being positioned into the growing filament.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural similarity data.

claim: A trypsinized fragment of Salmonella FliD that lacks the N-terminal 42 residues and C-terminal 51 residues can form pentamers but not decamers in solution and dissociates into smaller oligomers at low temperatures.
source: Previous analysis of a trypsinized fragment of Salmonella FliD that lacks the N-terminal 42 residues and C-terminal 51 residues, which is similar to the Pseudomonas FliD78–405 protein that we crystallized, showed that this fragment can form pentamers but not decamers in solution and dissociates into smaller oligomers at low temperatures (Vonderviszt et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Determinants outside of the head regions of FliD proteins of diverse bacteria control their oligomeric states.
source: This suggests that determinants outside of the head regions of FliD proteins of diverse bacteria control their oligomeric states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited Salmonella data and the current Pseudomonas data.

claim: Conformational flexibility in or relative repositioning of the head regions are not functional requirements of FliD.
source: Accordingly, we showed that FliD, when constrained to its hexameric state by disulfide bonds formed between neighboring head domain subunits, is fully functional in vivo. Thus,conformational flexibility in or relative repositioning of the head regions are not functional requirements of FliD but flexibility in regions outside of the head regions undoubtedly is.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data with the disulfide-locked hexamer.

claim: Flexibility in regions outside of the head regions is a functional requirement of FliD.
source: Thus,conformational flexibility in or relative repositioning of the head regions are not functional requirements of FliD but flexibility in regions outside of the head regions undoubtedly is.
evidence: This is an inference based on the oligomerization and HDX-MS data.

claim: The dependence of FliD oligomeric assembly on its flexible regions enhances the prospects of developing small molecule inhibitors of FliD oligomerization as a novel class of antibiotic agents.
source: Considering that inhibiting protein–protein interfaces with small molecules remains a major technical challenge (Arkin et al., 2014), the dependence of FliD oligomeric assembly on its flexible regions enhances the prospects of developing small molecule inhibitors of FliD oligomerization, and consequently of flagellar function, as a novel class of antibiotic agents.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the structural and functional data and cited knowledge about drug development challenges.
